title: Книжный клуб
desc:
В кабинете Хосе Луиса Арресе собрался его импровизированный "книжный клуб". Вокруг стола сгрудились стулья, а в тишине то и дело раздавался шорох карандашей. Мужчины с умным видом кивали, словно заправские философы. На столешнице среди блокнотов были разбросаны экземпляры нацистской литературы: от пресловутой "Майн кампф" до куда менее известных трудов. Они сосредоточенно подчёркивали нужные места, безжалостно вымарывая всё остальное.

В этих книгах была особая энергия, чуждая, тевтонская мощь, которую Арресе жаждал воссоздать и привить иберийской земле. В этом и заключалось главное преимущество изучения идеологии Гитлера: можно было отобрать самые полезные и действенные элементы его уродливого гибрида фашизма, отбросив всё лишнее, словно садовник, отделяющий здоровые плоды от гнилых.

И одним из таких гнилых плодов было презрение к католической церкви. Этого они перенять не могли. Конечно же, нет. Иберия - страна католическая до мозга костей. (Да, в Германии формально господствовал протестантизм, но нацисты также старались привить своей нации чуждое ей неоязычество). "Майн кампф" не станет их Библией. У них уже есть подлинник.

Однако что бы там ни говорили о нацистах, в эффективности им не откажешь. Гитлер был не просто политиком - он был воплощением германской воли, отлитым в граните. Настоящий вождь, фюрер. Арресе, даже встречавшийся с ним лично, думал о канцлере скорее как о явлении природы, чем как о человеке. Сможет ли он, Арресе, сравниться с ним? А если нет, то что нужно сделать, чтобы это стало возможным?

Испанский лидер откинулся на спинку стула. Жёсткая кожа недовольно скрипнула. Он потёр глаза, давая им отдохнуть от убористых готических букв, и нарушил молчание: "Запомните, друзья мои. Мы не немцы. И не итальянцы."

title: Лицом к солнцу
desc:
Утреннее солнце заливало школьный двор ярким светом, освещая детей, что выстраивались в ровные шеренги для своего ежедневного ритуала. Некоторым новая, с иголочки, форма строгого военного покроя казалась захватывающей, другие же с тоской теребили жёсткие воротники и красные нарукавные повязки, казалось, сжимавшие руки сильнее, чем нужно. Но кем бы они ни были - восторженными новобранцами или тихими страдальцами - все как один замерли, когда из громкоговорителя раздался скрежет первых аккордов "Cara al Sol".

Для измождённой учительницы это был сигнал подойти к основанию флагштока, держа в руках аккуратно сложенное полотнище. Дети молча следили, как флаг Фаланги медленно ползёт вверх, разворачиваясь на ветру: алый, золотой и снова алый на фоне ясного утреннего неба.

Попытка вскинуть руки в едином порыве провалилась: над головами вырос неровный лес дрожащих приветствий. Половина детей тут же чуть опустила ладони, превратив салют в козырёк от слепящего солнца. Остальные, щурясь, старались держать руку как положено, но их взгляды всё равно были устремлены не на флаг, а куда-то в сторону. Когда последние аккорды гимна замерли, по шеренгам пронёсся тихий вздох облегчения. Для ребёнка три минуты неподвижности - это вечность.

Сохраняя напускную строгость, ученики потянулись в здание школы под бдительными взглядами учителей. В каждом классе со стен на них взирали портреты Хосе Луиса Арресе и Примо де Риверы, требуя безмолвного почтения. Конечно, большинство детей не смогли бы сказать, кто из этих суровых мужчин Хосе, а кто - Примо, но раз уж они висят на стене, значит, люди важные.

title: Бойся цензора
desc:
Тусклая настольная лампа выхватывала из темноты лишь круг света на столе да склонившуюся над бумагами фигуру цензора. Он корпел над документами, одним росчерком пера верша судьбы нескольких примечательных произведений, изъятых в подполье. Почти всегда вердикт был один: запрет, сожжение, допросы владельцев - стандартная процедура. После долгих часов безмолвной работы он наконец добрался до последнего дела: книги, что ходила по рукам в группах сопротивления и была изъята во время недавнего рейда в трущобах Сарагосы.

Цензор методично листал страницы, делая пометки на полях. Перед ним был типичный сепаратистский трактат, густо приправленный коммунистическими идеями, - писанина, посягавшая на общественную мораль и подрывавшая авторитет Национального совета. Но любопытнее всего было другое: в этом экземпляре несколько имён были жирно зачёркнуты - жалкая, но отчаянная попытка уберечь от разоблачения тех, кого книга называла вождями.

Решение было очевидным. Запретить. Изъятые экземпляры - сжечь. Оставшиеся - найти и уничтожить. Прежде чем закончить работу, цензор сделал последнюю пометку: составить список всех известных владельцев книги для последующих допросов. Ведь подобная крамола не рождается из ничего. Если есть один источник, то при должной настойчивости и ресурсах можно раскрутить всю сеть.

title: Безмолвный мандат
desc:
Арресе знал один очень приём, которому его когда-то научили. Стоило лишь замолчать за кафедрой, и зал замирал, а напряжение в воздухе становилось почти осязаемым. Прежде он не верил в его силу, но теперь отчётливо ощущал эту энергию, исходящую от сотен лиц, застывших в ожидании его слова.

"Мы стали самодовольными," - наконец произнёс он, обводя взглядом членов Совета Фаланги. - "Возможно, этого и следовало ожидать. Возможно, такова судьба каждого великого государства."

Он подался вперёд, подставив лицо резкому свету прожектора. - "Но я хочу, чтобы каждый из вас - каждый политик, каждый солдат, каждый человек в этом зале - понял: это не война за сферы влияния, не война за ресурсы и не война за гордость. Это не далёкий конфликт, от которого можно отмахнуться."

Он выдержал ещё одну выверенную паузу. Зал был в его власти. - "В последний раз само наше существование оказывалось под такой угрозой во время Гражданской войны. Для большинства из вас те годы, 1936-й... 1939-й... всего лишь тема для разговоров. Но для меня это живая память, чьи отголоски звучат в бедах сегодняшнего дня. Поэтому я говорю вам: это война на выживание!"

Когда зал взорвался одобрительным гулом, Арресе позволил себе смягчить черты лица, приняв вид отца, которому предстоит сообщить тяжёлую весть. - "И именно поэтому мы обязаны мобилизовать всё: и армию, и экономику."

По лицам собравшихся пробежала тень тревоги. - "По опыту знаю, как непросто убедить людей вкладываться в армию," - произнёс он, словно рассуждая вслух. - "Почему? Потому что армия - как здоровье. Её истинную цену осознаёшь лишь тогда, когда она тебя подводит."

Он глубоко вздохнул и, опершись обеими руками о кафедру, обвёл зал тяжёлым взглядом.

description:
Арресе знал один очень приём, которому его когда-то научили. Стоило лишь замолчать за кафедрой, и зал замирал, а напряжение в воздухе становилось почти осязаемым. Прежде он не верил в его силу, но теперь отчётливо ощущал эту энергию, исходящую от сотен лиц, застывших в ожидании его слова.

"Мы стали самодовольными," - наконец произнёс он, обводя взглядом членов Совета Фаланги. - "Возможно, этого и следовало ожидать. Возможно, такова судьба каждого великого государства."

title: Спартак
desc:
The Sun was gone.

The world was gray around this abandoned highway, a dead layer of cloud seemingly lying over the sky. No rain fell, but the world seemed to hold its breath before a storm. Silence ruled; no cars seemed to come.

Slowly, a family moved along the battered highway with a pitiful cart of few provisions. The emptiness unnerved them, but they kept moving. To stay still was to die, their nervous eyes darting to any bit of sound. Such events were rare however - even animals seemed to have departed. Only a cold wind sometimes passing demonstrated any life in the world.

Except for the occasional panic at the soft breeze shifting a stone or the unexpected squeak of the sparse cart, they kept their eyes down to the ground. For all their days, weeks of walking they had received little news of the going of the War. Matters such as food and safety had taken far more precedence as they cowered in whatever makeshift shelters they could. In the desolate countryside, such things seemed rarer by the day.

The youngest in the family fell, a momentary stumble as their exhausted mind had a moment of dizziness. They lay dazed for a moment and as they stood back up they were forced to look upon their audience; the eyes that had followed them for miles.

From every light post, stretching far in both directions, bodies hung from the neck. Some wore symbols of the Republic. Some wore symbols of the Socialists. Others even wore the symbol of the so-called King. Around each neck was a sign, a sign which all the family tried to ignore as they shuffled forward. They knew not who hung them, but they feared them nonetheless.

title: Инферно
desc:
The first sign anything was wrong had been an ascending growl in the air. It had started subtle, unnoticed, but within minutes all the village could hear the roar growing louder.

They came over a nearby hill, metal monsters with stern-faced men hanging off their bodies. Their uniforms and equipment were dirty, caked in mud and grime, their eyes weary yet ablaze. They had not rested nor stopped as they had moved across the country and now they saw their target.

The people of the village immediately realized what they were. Some called for action, but there were no weapons or anyone to use them. Anyone who could fight had long since left. They began to flee, mothers dragging confused children out of houses while the old tried to hobble towards the fields.

The metal beasts came upon the town, and their rifles immediately shot anyone who ran. They locked the doors of stores and houses, before throwing prepared Zhdanovs through smashed windows onto any trapped inside.

Evil eyes looked upon any victim too slow to flee as they were dragged away. Screams came about as the beasts and men set upon anyone their rifles could catch in the fields and streets. Within an hour, little remained of the village except for burning houses, whimpers of the few living and the gunshot that silenced them. The soldiers rode away, talking and laughing amongst themselves.

From a single tree, that none of the monsters had thought to look in, a single child watched them leave.

title: Слёзы Мадрида
desc:
The rain poured relentlessly, the crack of thunder sounding like a whip upon the city. The column of liberators moved silently, illuminated only by the occasional spark from a damaged street lamp or strike of thunder.

The road slanted down, once beautifully paved but now broken and jagged. The area had been spared mass bombardment, but the bullet holes and uncollected corpses still riddled the paths to the side of the street, past a marching column. The flowing rainwater following the road washed over the bodies, twisted faces and broken limbs offering little resistance to the flow, but few of the marchers paid them any mind. They were too busy trying to keep their footing in the slippy torrent.

The only bodies free from the river were the few that hung from the windows. Dead from various means - though that was hard to tell in the twilight - with signs declaring they were the fate of all who betrayed Spain. A warning to the attackers and, perhaps, the defenders too.

What battle had been fought there, in that small street? The dead gave no answer, their resting places drowned in the cacophony of splashes that accompanied the troops. The empty sound bounced off the desolate tanned stone, no life appearing. For the living and the dead, none had for some time.

They walked in silence, as ghosts upon the nightly air, their gaunt eyes peering a way through the downpour. Their grim expressions betrayed a retreat into the mind they had all surrendered to. Where was the festivity of victory? Where was the adulation of liberation? Where was anyone? The cold and the water were the only indications of anything natural in the streets. Madrid's soul seemed absent, washed away. The sounds of recent conflict were gone, the blood lost in a river.

All that remained was silence.

title: Дети Гвадалахары
desc:
The center of the city was full of activity, trucks and men moving through with civilians trying their best to stay out of the way of both. Rifle cracks could still be heard over the city but they were organized and routine. Only the citizens paid them any mind.

Somewhere in the sprawl, a fountain square was abuzz with activity. A makeshift tent was set up in the corner with administration staff and supply officers trying to bring some order to all the newcomers. Men entered and left the chaos from all directions of the sunbaked square all day. One of these newcomers, a Sargento Ortiz, stumbled to the fountain exhausted from a day of walking. He was all that was left of his squad from the battle. He tried adjusting himself for merely a second however before his eye caught a child sitting across the empty basin.

More than one, two dozen children sat with their heads buried in their hands. Some of them seemed to sob while others sat completely still. The older ones wore oversized military jackets over casual clothes, while the younger ones had merely a military belt wrapped around them like a bandolier for military gear. Soldiers with rifles milled around them, unsure of themselves but clearly watching over them.

Ortiz, struck with curiosity, walked over to the nearest guard. "What's with the kids?" he asked.

The guard looked over the children morosely before he answered. "They wanted to use the kids. Bastards. Their officer ran off though."

Ortiz nodded. He'd seen such tactics before in the countryside. "That was lucky."

The guard looked at him, vexed at his nonchalance. He turned his head to look back at the kids, waving his rifle at Ortiz to move on. The Sargento complied.

title: Моя война в Сарагосе
desc:
The celebrations had continued late into the night, and despite the destruction many citizens had joined in the festivities. The last falange troops had been routed from the city, and despite the best efforts of some officers a spontaneous celebration had broken out among the citizenry and paramilitary units. Many of the organized troops soon followed.

Off the street, a lone soldier stumbled into an alley. His senses were dulled and his spirit high, precariously clutching a half empty bottle of bourbon. It wasn't usually his drink of choice but in the aftermath of battle there wasn't much choice. Men and women drank what could be found regardless of preference and they were glad for it.

The soldier was young, unused to the strong liquor. He made it halfway down the alley before stumbling onto the cold paving, dangerously close to vomiting. He held it in, dimly aware he was still wearing his military fatigues and unwilling to dirty them further. Out of the corner of his eye, a pair of boots slowly walked towards him from deeper in the alley.

"Soldier?" a gruff voice asked. The young soldier gleefully nodded, he'd been asked that so many times tonight and a drink often followed. He looked up. Above him was a man in a tattered outfit, civilian except for the jacket - which carried the emblem of the Falange.

The young soldier's breath hitched as he saw it. The gruff speaker knelt down and brandished a knife to the intoxicated soldier, gleefully watching the dull eyes light with terror. The knife was caked with dried blood.

"You celebrate your degeneracy winning prematurely," he whispered to the frozen soldier, "because not all of Spain's soldiers have left."

title: Руины Толедо
desc:
The dust had settled a few hours ago and the sun had started to set beside the collapsed cathedral. The previous night's bombardment had been terrible, the deep booms of the artillery muffling the screams as stone collapsed on those within. The cries had continued after the bombardment had ceased, and even now it seemed that in the eerie silence of the city that distress could be sensed. The sound however was elusive, caught only for a fleeting moment if it was there at all.

On a pile of rubble a woman sat. Her rags, barely clothes, were dust covered and gray from when she had crawled out from the ruin; seemingly the only one. She had been lucky, but unable to move away. At first the crescendo of shells had kept her huddled to the Cathedral, but now just numbness. She had wanted the cries of the trapped to stop, but now she wished for anything to break the silence.

The sounds of marching slowly approached, and with their rising volume so rose the woman. She had feared such sounds before but soldiers meant organized men, people who could help. Perhaps some could be saved? Through the devastated streets she watched the approaching Falange column. Before such a sight would have filled her with dread but now she welcomed them, rushing forwards despite her fatigue.

"Please, you have to help me," she pleaded with the column's Officer, desperately grabbing him and dragging him to the side. "There's people in the cathedral, we can still save some of them, we need to -"

A sharp slap silenced her, the officer then pushing her to the ground. "Out of the way" he said simply, rejoining the column which jeered at her mockingly. They threatened her with unspeakable things, mocked her missing friends and family; the column and the terror seemed endless as they passed by. They spared the cathedral no glance.

title: Воспоминания в Бадахосе
desc:
Carlos lay on the green grass, and for a moment the War had stopped.

The distant crackle and pops of sporadic gunfire sounded in the air, but the smell of the overgrown turf and the isolation of the area was a remedy that Carlos had not realized he needed. His mind hadn't felt so at ease in months. He lay relaxed, uncaring of his patrol for just a few minutes. It had been a hard road back to Badajoz. He could take a few moments for himself.

His father had brought him here, the Estadio El Vivero Stadium, to watch games before the War when he had been a boy. Watching those football games were some of his most cherished memories. His father had died in the early stages of the War, when the family had all tried to flee Badajoz due to his father's Falange associations, but the survival of the stadium meant that at least some of his father remained. Carlos hoped his father was smiling on him as their army had returned.

The serene image was sullied somewhat by a handful of bloated corpses sat against the side of the pitch. They were nude, their limbs the size of oil drums and the smell grotesque, but thankfully the smell didn't carry as far as Carlos. He had seen his fair share of corpses, and he knew better than to focus on such a ghastly sight. Instead, all he thought about was the warm sun on his face and the feel of the overgrown grass beneath him.

He would have to return to his patrol soon.After all, it was a one-man reconnaissance after the city was declared open; a vital task. His commanding officer had not shut up about that. He had been practically headhunted for it due to his familiarity with the area. However his eased mind was, for a moment, absent from practical military necessities.

A few more minutes of peace wouldn't hurt.

title: Стратегическая нейтрализация Картахены
desc:
They watched the distant blasts through the binoculars, a few kilometers from the artillery. The boom of the guns brought smiles to their faces as they saw the results, the hill upon which they stood offering an excellent vantage point.

Parts of Cartagena had survived relatively intact in the initial assault, on account of a lack of resistance. They noted with a hint of dark amusement that you could almost see the path the army had taken through the city, the ruin visible from any vantage point. The loss of such heritage saddened them, the thought of how much of Spain they had to destroy to save it hardly a happy thought, but their success offered ample condolence.

However, their men had continued to encounter resistance. A lone gunman perhaps? A suicide bomber? Even idiots practicing passive resistance, crossing roads before vital convoys. Though the organized enemies of Spain had been removed it seemed many of their corrupted denizens had yet to learn the lesson. A staffer, observing that certain undamaged districts seemed to have the most cases of such criminality, had offered this rather ingenious solution. As they watched another building fall they reflected on the message this would send to all remaining dissidents.

One officer, a career one rather than a wartime promotion like the rest of them, had voiced opposition to the plan by pointing out their orders were to utilize force effectively but proportionally. Fortunately he had been overruled, even if it was frustrating that he had refused to watch. Surely the men needed to see that they were all united?

They all collectively agreed to include his difficult attitude in their report.

description:
They watched the distant blasts through the binoculars, a few kilometers from the artillery. The boom of the guns brought smiles to their faces as they saw the results, the hill upon which they stood offering an excellent vantage point.

Parts of Cartagena had survived relatively intact in the initial assault, on account of a lack of resistance. They noted with a hint of dark amusement that you could almost see the path the army had taken through the city, the ruin visible from any vantage point. The loss of such heritage saddened them, the thought of how much of Spain they had to destroy to save it hardly a happy thought, but their success offered ample condolence.

However, their men had continued to encounter resistance. A lone gunman perhaps? A suicide bomber? Even idiots practicing passive resistance, crossing roads before vital convoys. Though the organized enemies of Spain had been removed it seemed many of their corrupted denizens had yet to learn the lesson. A staffer, observing that certain undamaged districts seemed to have the most cases of such criminality, had offered this rather ingenious solution. As they watched another building fall they reflected on the message this would send to all remaining dissidents.

One officer, a career one rather than a wartime promotion like the rest of them, had voiced opposition to the plan by pointing out their orders were to utilize force effectively but proportionally. Fortunately he had been overruled, even if it was frustrating that he had refused to watch. Surely the men needed to see that they were all united?

They all collectively agreed to include his difficult attitude in their report.

title: Глас народа в Кордове
desc:
They walked through the fogged streets, silent and aloof. They clutched their weapons and dark eyes looked through gas masks, surrounded by the stinging white smoke of tear gas. Behind them slowly trundled trucks, crudely redesigned for the machine guns strapped to their rears. Scattered around them were corpses. Some were caught beneath the wheels of the slowly moving trucks, creating sickening crunches and sharp bumps for the soldier operating the gun.All ignored them beyond a quick glance to verify death.

Occasionally, over the drone of the struggling, ill maintained engines they heard coughing. Someone who had played dead or wounded who had not yet bled out. Occasionally even someone clutching a weapon, perhaps hoping to make a defiant stand. The gas incapacitated all and the walking soldiers quickly dispatched them.

Some of them did so out of hatred, souls afire for the fools who had corrupted Spain. That even when defeated they continued to oppose their countries salvation. They pulled their triggers with satisfaction.

Others did it with pity. To see so many lost to the lies of monarchists, jews or communists - whoever this gathering had listened to - made them sad. So many good Spanish corrupted for foreign masters who cared nothing for them. They pulled their triggers with sadness.

Minutes earlier this street had been alive with shouting. None could remember whose slogans had been shouted and few of them cared. All it had taken was strategic use of tear gas and application of force to clear the way. Would the survivors who had successfully fled continue elsewhere? Maybe.

But today a message had been sent to Córdoba. Regardless of how the soldiers justified it to themselves, they hoped this would be the last time.

title: Союз, возрождённый во имя Его
desc:
Золотой град Испании. Сквозь сводчатые залы Ла-Клересии разносятся голоса - но сегодня здесь не поют псалмы и молитвы.

"Настал день нашего возрождения!" - тощий, как бич, человек вцепился в кафедру. Он вглядывался в лица собравшихся, где рядом с закалёнными ветеранами стояли совсем зелёные новобранцы - с тем же огнём в глазах, что и у старых бойцов. Или с тем же огнём, что лишь напоминает решимость, а на деле является юношеской наивностью.

"По милости Господней... и по крови, пролитой братьями нашими, мы вновь стали хозяевами этой земли." - Оратор быстро осенил себя крестом, и снова взялся за речь. - "Однако мы ещё не покончили со всеми предателями полуострова."

"Теперь нам необходимо разобраться с главными попирателями нашего священного порядка - португальскими лжецами!" - его голос прокатился по рядам, вызывая в ответ сначала низкий ропот, а потом и рык. - "Они лгали! Лгали прямо нам в лицо! Лгали до тех пор, пока марксистская нечисть в Стране Басков не взялась за оружие! Тогда-то португальцы и показали своё истинное лицо - предателей, готовых бросить нас на съедение в крестовом походе против безбожных выродков!"

Крики взметнулись к куполу. Захлопали выстрелы, засвистели пули, рикошетя от стен дома Божьего. Сотни ног застучали по каменным плитам проходов, набирая темп, наливаясь яростью - но всё это было лишь жалкой тенью по сравнению с Гневом самого Всевышнего.

"Все, кто ещё не смирился с нашим праведным правлением, должны преклонить колена перед волей Испанского национального совета! Только в этой войне, и нигде больше, обретут они спасение от коммунистического ярма и иноземного ига - дабы вернуться в лоно нашего Святого Союза!"

options.name: Во имя Отца, и Сына, и Святого Духа.
